utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you're back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm happy to see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness formerly had protective measures and the Prosecution is at this time going to move to amend those protective measures based upon the wishes of the witness, so if I might introduce Steven Cole to the Chamber. He will be handling this witness and will deal with that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cole.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. This witness, as has been indicated, was granted protective measures in the Vasiljevic trial. The witness is prepared during these proceedings to testify openly and I would ask that the protective measures previously in place be revoked so that he can testify in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have no difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour, sir. The witness is Mr. Huso Kurspahic, and I ask that he called to testify. He's a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Before you bring the witness in, let me just without to give a decision on some 92 ter applications. On the 15th of February of this year, the Prosecution filed a motion requesting that the trial testimony and witness statements of several witnesses be admitted into evidence under Rule 92 ter. On the 8th of August, the Prosecution filed a supplemental motion pursuant to the same Rule in which it requested leave to add several witness statements to its existing 92 ter witness material. The Defence of Sredoje Lukic responded to the Prosecution's motion on the 28th of February. Defence of Milan Lukic responded on the 28th of March. Neither Defence responded to the 8th of August motion. On Monday, the 25th of August, the Trial Chamber issued an oral decision in respect of both motions insofar as they related to the following witnesses: VG-022, VG-011, VG-097, VG-104, and VG-061. The Chamber remained seized of the motions in relation to the remaining seven witnesses, namely VG-003, VG-018, VG-025, VG-038, VG-071, VG-078, and VG-084. The Chamber has reviewed the evidence submitted in the two motions with regard to the seven witnesses under consideration. It finds that the transcripts, the statements, and associated exhibits are admissible under Rule 92 ter once the requirements of that Rule are met, and that disposes of both motions. Let the witness be brought in. Mr. Cole, how long do you intend to spend on this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: I'm hoping, sir, that approximately half an hour, the allowable time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Cole.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Mr. Kurspahic. Can you hear clearly?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes, I can hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Could you please state your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: My name is Huso Kurspahic. I was born on the 11th of May, 1950, in the village of Koritnik, Visegrad municipality, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: During the spring of the year 1992, in which municipality did you live?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I lived in the municipality of Visegrad, and I worked in the area of Visegrad and the local commune of Medjedja.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Kurspahic is a 92 ter witness, and I'll now proceed to confirm his prior statement, his prior testimony and the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Mr. Kurspahic, did you give a statement to an ICTY investigator on the 12th of May, 2000, and could I just ask you --

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Mr. Kurspahic, could I ask that you don't refer to those documents in front you while I'm asking you these questions, please.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I won't be doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And the statement that you gave was on the 12th of May, 2000?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And can you confirm that the statement was typed in English at the time, it was then read back to you in Bosnian, and you signed the English version?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity last week here at the Tribunal to review that statement in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Now, was there one matter which you wished to correct in that statement, namely the name of your nephew who perished in the fire at Pionirska Street, Visegrad, on the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. His name was Faruk, not Enver. That was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And the surname was Sehic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Now, with that correction, do you confirm that the statement you made on the 12th of May, 2000, is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I tender the statement of Mr. Kurspahic into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter. It is the statement dated 12 May 2000, and the 65 ter number is 169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P36, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Mr. Kurspahic, do you confirm that you testified over two days during the Mitar Vasiljevic trial in 2001, those days being 19 September and 24 September 2001?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity last week to listen to the audio recordings of your testimony in the Mitar Vasiljevic trial?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Was that testimony true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Do you need to make any corrections to it?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I tender the transcripts of the witness's testimony into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The transcript from 19 September 2001, 65 ter number 122; the transcript from 24 September 2001, 65 ter number 123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 122 will become Exhibit number P37. 65 ter number 123 will become Exhibit P38.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Thank you. At this point also, Your Honours, I would ask that an exhibit which accompanied the witness's testimony and was produced as an exhibit in the Vasiljevic trial be tendered into evidence in this trial pursuant to Rule 92 ter. This is a list of 51 names of victims of the Pionirska Street fire and the 65 ter number is 170.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 170 will become Exhibit number P39, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And Your Honours I will deal with a correction to that list of names at this stage and could I ask that the list of 51 names, Exhibit P39, please be shown to Mr. Kurspahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Mr. Kurspahic, can you see the list of 51 names on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Would you look at number 37 on the list. Is that the name Hasib Kurspahic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: That's my father, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And can you confirm that in fact your father Hasib Kurspahic survived the Pionirska fire?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: For some time after the Pionirska fire did you believe that in fact your father had died during that fire together with your mother, your two sisters, your nephew, and many other relatives?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I believed that because it was impossible for him to escape the fire on his own because at the time he was 70 years of age, he was a sick person, and that is why I believed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And did you subsequently find out that your father had in fact survived that fire, and did you meet up with him again in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I learned this through ham operators that he had survived, that he was in Visoko, the village of Mosce and I visited him in 1993 and that was my first contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kurspahic, last week were you able to view a videotape of an interview with your father which took place in 1992 shortly after the Pionirska fire?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And did you confirm that that videotape interview of your father was produced into evidence during your testimony at the Vasiljevic trial in 2001?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only about ten seconds. There was just an image of my father. I was asked, "Is this your father?" I said, "Yes," and then it was finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would ask that the videotape interview of this witness's father in 1992 which accompanied the witness's testimony and was produced as an exhibit in the Vasiljevic trial be tendered into evidence in this trial pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The 65 ter number is 119.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will become Exhibit P40.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And along with the actual videotape itself I would ask at this point that the transcript of the video interview of the witness's father in English and B/C/S be tendered into evidence also pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The English transcript is 65 ter number 120, and the B/C/S transcript of the videotape interview is 65 ter number 121.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 120 will become Exhibit P41. 65 ter number 121 will become Exhibit P42, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Mr. Kurspahic, can you confirm that it was your father whom you could see and hear being interviewed on that videotape?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I'm going to provide the witness with some pseudonym sheets. They are -- well, the pseudonym sheet, it is not in respect of this witness but in respect of three persons who he may refer to during his testimony so that he knows the pseudonym numbers to refer to rather than the witness's name. If I could provide the witness with that, and a copy, of course, for the Defence and the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Sir, I have the three pseudonyms on the one sheet. Is there any problem with it being dealt with that way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have three on one sheet, and the three who are to be referred to are those three.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kurspahic, I have given to you -- I have provided to you a pseudonym sheet, not for yourself but in the event you need to refer to the three persons listed therein, in which case I would ask you to use the pseudonym numbers alongside the names rather than the names themselves.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: I'm going to just refer again to the list of 51 names that you viewed a short time ago. During the previous trial you made some corrections to the surnames of three of the names on that list, and you added three other names during your testimony in the Vasiljevic trial. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Now, apart from your father, have you ever seen or heard from any of these persons on the corrected list since the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I use this, because I have this list in front of me?

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Could I just -- maybe I didn't make myself understood. Could I just ask you the question again. Putting your father aside, his name is on the list currently, have you seen or heard from any of those other persons on the list since 1992?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: No. I do apologise. I didn't understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the list at present includes your mother, your two sisters, and your nephew?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: How many others on that list with the surname Kurspahic are related to you?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: All of them. We are all related. Some of them are distant relatives, some are close relatives. This is one family.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And through the inquiries that you have subsequently made, what do you believe now to be the total or approximate total number of persons who perished in the Pionirska fire on the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: There is no accurate number, but there would be about 70 people who perished there.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to the videotape interview of your father, can you confirm that that depicts your father describing this fatal fire and how he escaped from it?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: What date was it that you met up with your father after the fire in 1993?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 24th of January, 1993. It was in Visoko. I'm not quite sure, but that's what it says. Yes. Yes. 23rd or 24th. You can read that from my statement, and I stand by what is written in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And what date did your father say to you that the Pionirska fire occurred? On what day did it occur?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell me the date. This is what he said exactly: On the fourth day of Bajram in Visegrad, and Bajram lasts and you celebrate it for four days, so that would be the 14th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And who did your father say were the main perpetrators who killed your family members during the fire?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: My father told me that on that date this was done by Sredoje Lukic, Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and Bosko Djuric was seen nearby, then Zoran Joksimovic, a man with the last name Susnjar, Zoran Joksimovic, and another individual with -- a blonde with white complexion with long hair, and he was Milan Lukic's escort. Nobody knows his exact name. There were a total of seven men who arrived in front of the house on Pionirska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kurspahic, were you asked by your father to solemnly swear to do something as his dying wish?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. My first encounter with him, he started crying when he saw me, and he said, "I leave it up to you to tell about what happened on that day in Pionirska Street in Visegrad since I am sick and old and I probably won't live long enough to see the freedom." He left it to me, and I gave him my word that I would do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Now, you were the -- the head of the police station in Medjedja when you first heard of the Pionirska fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: No. I was the commander of the reserve police administration. I was not the chief. I was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: All right. So who was the first person that told you about the Pionirska fire? And please use the pseudonym if the name is on the sheet in front of you.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: The first time I heard about this event was from Witness VG-013.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: How long after the Pionirska fire did she tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I couldn't be precise, but I think it was seven or eight days after the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes. And did VG-13 tell you that she was a survivor of the Pionirska fire like your father?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Now, at Medjedja did you also meet the survivor of another house fire, the Bikavac fire, which also occurred in Visegrad in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just, a minute. Don't answer. Mr. Cepic is on his feet. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think all of these questions -- most of these questions have the character of leading questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Who was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm inclined to agree that they are a little bit leading so you have to be careful about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Now, at Medjedja did you meet the survivor of another house fire in Bikavac, the Bikavac fire which occurred sometime in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Who was that person, and please refer to them by the pseudonym if the name is on the sheet in front of you.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: That person is VG-114. She came to Medjedja all bandaged up. She exuded a bad smell. She had been badly burnt on her face and hands as well. She told me there had been a fire in Visegrad in a street called Bikavac near Kopito in the house of Meho Alic, where around 72 persons had perished in the fire. She was the only survivor. She was hardly able to speak. That statement, that first statement, was videotaped, and I believe that this videotape is stored at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Were you able to assess how long after the fire incident it was that you spoke with her?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I think again seven or eight days later. Her body was an open wound. Everything, face, hands, body was covered with wounds that exuded such a bad smell that you couldn't come practically any closer to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Who did she say were the persons responsible for causing these injuries to her and the other people?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: She only mentioned Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and Mitar Vasiljevic, saying that it was them who had set the house on fire. They were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Now, last week during your proofing you were shown copies of five documents that had been provided to the Prosecution by the Milan Lukic Defence. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And these were documents of the style of Visegrad police documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I haven't got any objections to those documents yet but I just object because I haven't got any announcement that the OTP will use those documents. I haven't got -- received any information, supplemental information sheet or something similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cole, is that so? As you know, you're required to --

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- provide timely notification.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: I'm reasonably confident that we did send a notification. It's just one of those documents I'm going to be referring the witness to. I wonder if I could just check with the case manager, sir. I personally was looking after this and asked that a message be sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, do so quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Sir. Yes. It's been suggested, and can I put it this way, sir, I'm able to proceed in the absence of that document by asking questions around it. Once we have found the confirmation that's been supplied to the Defence, we can deal with it then, in fact, and on the screen if there's no further objection. So with your permission, sir, I'll continue to ask questions about the document. It may be that we can deal with -- without producing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kurspahic, I'm going to ask you about just one of those documents that your shown last week. It was a document that contained a list of 15 names of persons, and it purported to be the list of 15 police officers sent from Visegrad to Kopito on the 13th of June, 1992. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as some background to these questions, were you a policeman at Visegrad and Medjedja for a number of years?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: From when until when were you a police officer there?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Correct, the 1st of January, 1970, until I fled from Visegrad on the 6th of April, 1992. That was the last day I was in Visegrad, and I was on active duty all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Do you recall last week when you looked at the list of the 15 names that you saw the name Milan Lukic at number 4 on the list?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, was Milan Lukic a police officer in Visegrad or anywhere else at any time, to the best your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection, lack of foundation. The witness testified that he left the police department in Visegrad the 2nd of April -- or 6th of April. This document post dates that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you laid a foundation, Mr. Cole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, don't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Well, sir, the document, as I've indicated and as the witness has confirmed, has a list of 15 names. Certainly the date is the 13th of June, but as far as he is able to with his experience, he's quite entitled, with respect, to say that he knew or didn't know that a person who was named on the list was or wasn't a police officer. Now, the fact that he was a police officer till the 6th of April doesn't exclude him from commenting on or answering the question that he's just been asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to answer that question whether from your own knowledge or from information that you've acquired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am. Until two days before when I heard about it, I didn't know that he had ever been on the police force, any police force. It's very true, though, there was a court case in Bosnia-Herzegovina against Zeljko Lalek, where the same question was asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you just tell us whether you know and how you know it. Just concentrate on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milan had never been on the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Kurspahic, at the time that you left the police in April 1992 what was the total number of police officers, both regular and reserve police officers, at that time?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, on active duty there were 31 officers, and together with the reserve policemen there were a total of 200 or 220 for the whole municipality, because you have to take into account that there were six reserve police administrations -- or, rather, police stations in addition to the police station in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: So just to clarify then, at the time that you left in April 1992, at that time had you ever heard any suggestion that Milan Lukic was a police officer in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I had never heard any such thing, and he wasn't a police officer. You have to understand, people, this was a small town in which I knew everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you about Mr. Sredoje Lukic, and was he a colleague of yours in the police in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: How many years were you colleagues, a colleague of Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: At least eight to ten years. Ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: How many years is it since you last saw Mr. Sredoje Lukic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm seeing Sredoje Lukic here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Can you see him here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Just hold it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, we do not dispute that Mr. Kurspahic knows Sredoje Lukic, but this method of identification in the courtroom is something we do dispute in general and in principle, because in decisions in the Vasiljevic and Limaj cases this particular method of evaluation -- of identification has already been evaluated. That is the basis for my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In a situation where the witness is saying that he knew him for ten years before, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I said, we do not challenge the fact that Mr. Kurspahic knows Sredoje Lukic. I just object on principle to this form of identification in the courtroom, also in light of possible further situations like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kurspahic, you said earlier, "This is the first time I'm seeing Sredoje Lukic here in the courtroom." Do you remember saying that a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Where can you see him here in the courtroom, please?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: In the last row, the second person from the policeman. The first next to the coloured officer wearing headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes. Any other description? Let's just make it clear the person you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, there is Sredoje Lukic. I'm looking at him, and he's looking at me. You can ask him if he knows me. We are being confronted. That's why I wanted to testify, so I can say these things in their faces in public, that I wouldn't be saying anything behind anyone's back. I wanted to say all I know from A to Z. That is Sredoje Lukic, my former colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And just to make it clear for the record, Mr. Kurspahic, was it the man sitting down or the man standing up that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: The man who stood up, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: The record could indicate that the accused Sredoje Lukic stood up at that stage. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And just a couple more questions, Mr. Kurspahic. Do you have a brother called -- did you have a brother called Osman Kurspahic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Is he still alive today?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: When did you last see him alive or hear from him?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: The last time I saw him was in Korfica [phoen] village. I don't know the exact date when the army marched into Visegrad. He came with another man to Kabotica [phoen] village where I was with my unit, and that's when I saw him for the last time, and he returned to the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: What year would that have been?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: 1992. I think the first half of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: And did you -- did you subsequently receive some information about what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: What did you hear -- what did you hear happened to him?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: He was executed. First he was detained at the police administration in Visegrad, and after that, as I learnt, he was taken to the Uzamnica military barracks in Visegrad, and that's where he was executed, as I learned, and if you want to know from whom I learned it, it was Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I found the information about the advice to the Defence that the document, the list of 15 names, would be referred to during the examination-in-chief. An e-mail was sent on Friday, the 29th of August, at 3.53 p.m. advising that this document would form part of the examination-in-chief. So I'm wondering on that basis if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: I suppose, sir, it's just a matter of it being -- well, in fact the witness has referred to it. I don't think we need, sir, any further -- spend any time on it. The witness covered it without referring to the list of 15 names, so I'm intent to leave it at that, sir. It will be a Defence exhibit. For the record, Y019-1568. It's a document that was supplied to the Prosecution, but it doesn't have a 65 ter number, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COLE
utterances.text: So those are my questions. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kurspahic. Good afternoon, Mr. Kurspahic.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: My name is Jason Alarid and I'm representing Mr. Milan Lukic here today. May I ask a few questions about your memories?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The first thing I would like to discuss with you is the structure of the police and your experience with the police as you left in April 1992. Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, at the time you left Visegrad, what was your position specifically?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I was the commanding officer of the police administration in Medjedja, and that's where I was the whole time. I went there and continued working there as an active-duty policeman, commanding officer, that is komandir, of the reserve police administration in Medjedja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the reserve police administration what is the difference to you between an active-duty police officer and a reserve-duty police officer?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: An active-duty police officer wore a uniform of one kind, and reserve police officers wore different uniforms from a different material. We received a salary and they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please describe the differences in the uniforms, please.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: The active police had blue uniforms, and the reserve police uniforms were homespun cloth, also blueish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did anyone wear camouflage uniforms as a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: In my area, in my detachment, no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And your detachment, was it debanded when the police force broke up into Serb and Muslim partitions?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were in Medjedja. We no longer gravitated towards Visegrad, and, yes, they were disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And why did you know longer gravitate toward Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not our purpose to gravitate towards Visegrad. Our area was the local commune of Medjedja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that local commune was a Muslim commune. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was it a mixed community?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was mixed. I have a whole study, if you want me to elaborate on this. There were 91 per cent Muslims and 9 per cent Serbs and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did it stay that way after the fighting began or did the Serbs move away?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: No, it did not stay that way. The Serbs left the police administration ten days before the war broke out. They walked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what was the police administration before the war broke out? Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I was the commanding officer, komandir, and Sine [phoen] Furtula, a Serb, was my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And as the commander officer are you saying you had jurisdiction over the 220 reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: That's not true. Maybe you misunderstood me. In total the police administration with six local communes had reserve and active police officers around 220 or perhaps 250 with a full complement. That was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you're including at this time the active-duty officers, of which you mentioned there were 31?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And as commander you said you were commander of the reserve force. Did you have 220 men under your control, or was that divided by the five communities -- or six communities?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Sir, I definitely had 51 officers in the local commune of Medjedja. I commanded 51 active police officers. Two hundred twenty was the total number for the municipality of Visegrad. I think I was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when it broke up how many Muslims were there and how many Serbs were there?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I've said there were only Muslims. We were 47, and there were four Serbs in total, including the deputy commander, and they all walked out of their jobs ten days before the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yet would it -- would it be fair to say that the Serb side of the police force still considered themselves active duty and working?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they continued to work in Visegrad. Most likely they did, but they no longer worked in Medjedja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be fair also that you wouldn't have had access to the Serbian police force records considering that you were in Medjedja?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I had no access from the moment the Serb police force was established. I've never seen those files.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that a police force is something where new hires do come on, and also this was a time of war so there might have been people being conscripted or drafted into the police force?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And were there opportunities where you on the Muslim side drafted and conscripted people into the police force in order to keep order?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not then, not at that time at the beginning. It was in September 1992 that some new officers joined my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you would have no knowledge of new officers that joined the Serbian side of the police force. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Correct. I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you wouldn't have any knowledge here to give the Court today whether or not Milan Lukic might have been hired after you left in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I've made a statement that I had never heard until two days ago that Milan Lukic had ever been a policeman, active or reserve duty, in that republic, and you can check and compare my statement with the statements of policemen who have testified in the court case against Lalek Zeljko at the state court in Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo. There are three of those witnesses. If you need their names I'll give them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: And they emphatically said that Milan Lukic had never been on the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you have their names?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What are their names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we ask the witness the names may we make some inquiry as to whether these witnesses may be under protective measures in the Sarajevo court or take it in closed session to -- in the event that there might be that chance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Who would know if they are under protection? Mr. Alarid wouldn't know, but so -- I believe that out of an abundance of caution, let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can make a phone call later today, Your Honour, to verify whether they are or not and then maybe amended the Court's order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: We're in private session, sir. Can you name those witnesses, please?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: If the Court permits me to say that, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Darinko Savic, a desk officer still working at the Visegrad police administration. She was a desk officer in the passport department. The next one was Miladina Uljarevic. She was in charge of the personnel department in Visegrad while I was there working there. I don't know whether she's still working there or not. And the third witness was inspector Boban Tomic, a police inspector. He has retired in the meantime as I understand, and he lives in Visegrad, as all of them do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you don't have any real idea of whether these people were working at the police department during the early months, the spring of 1992, do you?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: What people?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The three witnesses you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were working and they're still working except for Boban, who has retired. Miladina, I'm not sure about, but Dara definitely is working.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Working today doesn't necessarily mean they were working in June of 1992 since that was during the war.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Sir, they were working all the time with me for ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you had no access to the Serbian side of the police force after April 1992. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can go back to public session now. Just a minute, please. Witness, just a minute. Let us return to open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed now, Witness, with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know an officer Momir Lakic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Momir Lakic was never a policeman in Visegrad. That is to say while I was there I had never heard of him being one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you're not aware that over a hundred new reserve police officers were put into place after the break-up of the Serbian and Muslim police force?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you're a police officer. Why wouldn't you be interested in what the Serbian side was doing?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in that specific aspect, whether they have reached the required manpower levels. That was somebody else's concern, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What are the required manpower levels according to your standard procedures?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: In Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Previously it was between 220 and 250 of both active and reserve-duty officers as a municipality. I wasn't involved in this particular area, and I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: After the break-up of the police department do you have knowledge of who became commander of the police force?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who was that? Who was the commander of the police force, sir?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Dragan Tomic, who used to be an inspector while I was in active service, and after the Muslims left and the dissolution of the police force, Dragan Tomic came on board. I heard that he was killed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And who was the chief of the police force?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I have certain information that Risto Perisic was appointed head of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't true that it would have been the Crisis Staff that would have appointed Mr. Perisic to head of the police administration?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Listen, I don't know about that. This is not my area. These are political issues. I am involved in police work. Who is being appointed and how, I really cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you must bear that in mind. The witness says he doesn't have any knowledge in that area. Let's move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So what you're saying, sir, is that the appointment of these officials became a political matter at that time?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You are now trying to provoke me here. I came here -- give me specific questions. I've told you I don't know. Do you need anything else from me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, I have some sympathy for the witness. He has said he doesn't know anything about these matters, so move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know a police officer named Vidoje Andric?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Tell me about your knowledge of Mr. Andric.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vidoje Andric was a reserve policeman while I was in the Visegrad police administration. I have heard that he was killed in a car along with Dragan Tomic, Vidoje Andric, Milutin's son, I don't know his name, and another person in the village of Okrugla near Visegrad, that they drove over a mine, an anti-tank mine on the road that had been planted by the Serbs to prevent the Muslims from reaching the bridge, because there were about 800 Muslims -- Muslim refugees in the forest near the village of Okrugla.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was the date of this mine incident?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I know that it was the first half of 1992, because sometime in July these refugees managed to cross over to the free territory, actually to Medjedja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you indicated on direct exam that this was a small town and you knew everyone; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But you did not know Milan Lukic; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Not much, because he left Visegrad a long time ago. I used to know him when he was a little boy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how did you know him as a little boy? How old was he the last time you could say you saw Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I think it was the time when he attended elementary school. If you want me to explain how I knew him, I can do that. At the time I was an active-duty policeman in Kamenica village where a Centrotrans bus from Visegrad was parked. Milan broke into that bus, and I as the commander of that sector, Milos Mandic, carried out the on-site investigation, and that was the last time I saw him, and that is when I became acquainted with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you know his family?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you know who his father was? Mile?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I know Milan. He was working in the forestry department. I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I said Mile, not Milan.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: His father, Mile. I think I also didn't say Milan. I think we understand each other well. However, I can repeat if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you know a police officer Milovan Vilaret?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: No. I know that there is only one Vilaret household in the area of Visegrad, definitely only one household.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you don't know Milovan?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you -- in this particular case you gave several statements and those have been introduced into evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: What are you referring to? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you also reviewed your father's videotaped interview on the television?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you review the transcript in B/C/S of the interview?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you read that in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, do you realize that in that particular interview with the journalist your father does not make mention of any of the names of the accused except Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he did not mention anything about rapes occurring during his detention there. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: He said in his interview that he didn't know about rapes, and that is what I read.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he also indicated in his interview that he did not know the young men who had detained him. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the only reference that he made to Mitar Vasiljevic was that Mujo had received a piece of paper giving him safe passage. Isn't that true? Isn't that true, sir, that Mujo had gotten a piece of paper from Mitar Vasiljevic setting out that he would receive no harm?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: That's what it says in my father's statement. That's what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he gave this statement pretty close after the incident, in July of 1992. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And yet in your later statements you indicate that your father -- and how old was your father at the time of the incident?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: He was 70. So he was born in 1990 -- 1919. So if my mathematics is okay, 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he died in what year, sir?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: In 1996, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you indicated in your statement that you had spoken with him on five or six occasions between 1992 and 1996?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, because we had lived together. From 1995 onwards until he died we lived together in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when did you retire from the police force?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of January, 1998, from the Centar police administration in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was that a promotion of sorts to go to Sarajevo from the smaller community of Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in that. I had kidney problems at the time. I was airlifted by helicopter to Sarajevo. If this Honourable Court would allow me to say, I was supposed to go to Germany to work as a security officer, but I wasn't able to leave Gorazde for 11 months. I was transferred from Gorazde. I have papers to support that, and I officially joined the Centar police administration in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: As a police officer for several decades, was it your responsibility to do long-term criminal investigations?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: That's an integral part of police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is an integral part of police work filing police reports, taking statements?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And being a police officer is really a 24-hour-a-day job. You come to work when the need arises. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And yet you never filed formal police reports and statements on behalf of your father in the investigation of the Pionirska Street fire. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? File where?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, according to you, you had specific information through your father and other witnesses, essentially VG-114 about both the fires of Bikavac and Pionirska Street. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in -- but you did not file any formal police reports in accordance with your duties as a police officer after speaking with his witnesses. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: That's not true, sir. If necessary, I can explain. I took statements and other numerous statements. After the fall of Medjedja I set all the records on fire in order to prevent them from getting into the hands of the Serbs. It fell on the 31st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When, sir, the 31st of May?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: That is the date when Medjedja fell, and I think I set the documentation on fire that very same night.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: 31st of May when?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: 1993, and the other one I set on fire in Medjedja when the army entered, and that would be on the 14th -- give me a second. The 14th of April, 1992. I had some papers. I set them on fire in Medjedja when the Uzice and the Romanija Corps arrived in the area of Visegrad municipality. These are -- were former JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Why not forward your investigation to Sarajevo where larger authorities could take action?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: There were no communications, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you realize that if you set them on fire in Medjedja in 1992 that was before the dates of the fires that we're talking about here today?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: That was only part of the records. It does not refer to the ones referring to taking criminal statements and things like that, and you wouldn't be interested in those papers, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No. The papers I'm interested in are direct investigations relating to the Pionirska Street fire or the Bikavac fire. Those are the papers we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: A report rather than a statement was written by me, and I set both reports on fire on the 31st of May, 1993, when I left the area of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And yet you waited until March 20th of 1994, more than two years -- or almost two years after the fire to give your next statement. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Who shall I file it to, sir? I was the main man in the area. We were surrounded. There was no way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But yet in 1994, it was the first time you made authorities in Sarajevo aware of the fact that you believed -- or in fact you told them your father reported that Milan Lukic, Sredoje Lukic, and Mitar Vasiljevic committed the fire in Pionirska Street. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: That is true, but not in Sarajevo. It was in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Gorazde. I apologise. And you also indicated in that statement that your father had -- had indicated that a rape had occurred and named a name. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But in the statement given by your father to the journalist just a month after the incident, he made no mention of knowledge of any rapes or even knowledge of the identities of any of the named accused other than Mitar Vasiljevic. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: That is true, but you have to look at this man, how he looked like after this tragedy in which 70 of his neighbours and relatives, including his wife, were burned. He lost two daughters and two sons. He was held captive in Visegrad. Please put yourself in his position. He was seriously ill. What kind of statement would you, sir, give if you were in his shoes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, if I witnessed or knew of a rape, I might say I knew of a rape.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection as to relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is a rhetorical question illustrated that way. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in your statement to the ICTY in the year 2000, was that the next time after 1994 you gave an interview addressing the fires on Pionirska Street or Bikavac?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you realize that there's no mention of your contact with VG-114 or the Bikavac fire in your 2000 statement to the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: It is possible, but I'm here now, and I can tell you. Ask me anything you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, the one thing I'd like to ask you is excluding what people told you or what you heard, you really know absolutely nothing about the Pionirska Street fire or the Bikavac fire. This all came second-hand to you. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And isn't it true that over time your statement has changed and you have added names to your father's statement since he gave it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I gave the statement in which I repeated what he had told me. I don't know what he said earlier, nor had I had an opportunity to see what he stated earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, in your statement of 3 -- or excuse me, March 20th, 1994, you only named four names -- excuse me, three names in relation to the Pionirska Street fire. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You have my statement. You can check whether it's correct, and I cannot confirm that until I look at my statement. You should be aware of how a long time has elapsed since.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, by the time we get to 2000, you've added and you've implied that seven people were directly responsible for the fire in Pionirska Street.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: There's mention of seven men being there at the time. Some were nearby the house. The three or four of them, Milan, Sredoje and Mitar entered the house while the rest were in the yard, Bosko, Lalco, Susnjar and the reported teacher Milan, according to my father, and I gave my statement on the basis of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you realize that a trial has occurred in this case in the matter of Mitar Vasiljevic, and it's already been concluded?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you realize at that trial Mitar Vasiljevic proved that he had in fact broken his leg and could not have been anywhere in Visegrad after 8.00 p.m. in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection. I'm not sure that's relevant nor am I sure that's a fair characterisation of what the Trial Chamber found in that case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the point of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The point of the question is -- is he's taking from a hearsay perspective what his father said about people's involvement of fire that went into the late evening. In fact, all other reports say the fire started close to midnight. The Trial Chamber found that Mitar Vasiljevic could -- checked himself into the hospital around 9.30 in the evening and I believe the 8.00 p.m. reference I made was relating the time it would take someone from actually breaking their leg to get to the hospital. And so in that fact it was impossible for Mitar Vasiljevic to have been at the scene of the fire that evening at the late night hours, early morning hours of the fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would seem to me that if -- I mean the Chamber today has the task of evaluating this witness's evidence. It seems to me if Mr. Alarid is saying that this other -- the findings of the Bench in Mitar Vasiljevic is evidence that should be used in this court, then a motion for adjudicated facts should be made. It's also inaccurate what is being said about the case. The Trial Chamber in Mitar -- in the Mitar Vasiljevic case found that Mitar Vasiljevic was present at the Pionirska Street location and was instrumental in getting those people to stay there and did provide a document. Again information that is corroborated by the -- the witness here today with respect to what his father has told him, but the Prosecution hasn't stood up here and -- and said to the witness, well, this is what the Trial Chamber found in this other case. I believe it's irrelevant what the Trial Chamber found to the task that the Chamber is engaging in in this present trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what the Trial Chamber found in the Mitar Vasiljevic case in relation to this particular matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's -- thank you. He doesn't know. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: If that -- hypothetically speaking, sir, if it were shown that Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic were not able to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the line you're pursuing now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, the line is that again this is second-hand information, and maybe certain people he spoke to were mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so, sir, if it was discovered that Mitar Vasiljevic broke his leg in the early evening hours of the date of the fire and could not have been present when it started, would that mean that certain people you spoke to were in fact mistaken or assumed something that was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow that. Don't answer that, Witness. I'm not allowing that question. It's not for the witness to say what is in people's minds or how they would view that particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And this, Your Honour, as an American lawyer this provides one those peculiar situations of which when so much hearsay is allowed to be extrapolated upon of course with the Court being able to take into consideration the weight of any particular set of evidence, it is difficult for me to cross-examine this when in fact this witness's understanding the fire came completely from someone else's understanding. So essentially allowing him to testify via 92 ter and also reaffirm that today, you are allowing him to say that his father understood X, Y, and Z, let's say, and if I'm not allowed to at least challenge that but sort of put it to the witness as you say, that is really -- you know, where else can I do that, because there was a trial finding of fact related to the ability of Mr. Vasiljevic to both be at the Bikavac fire and the Pionirska Street fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, I'll tell you where else you can do that. You can do it in your submissions to us and ask us to attach very little or no weight to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour. I just -- it's hard for me to put it to the witness any other way. That's I guess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Ah, we have passed the time for the break. Let us break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you have about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Fifteen or 50, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Fifteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mr. Kurspahic, I'd like to ask you about a few names and ask you if you recognise them of members of the reserve police force as you left in April of 1992. Do you know a Nenad Tanaskovic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: He used to be a ticket controller in Centrotrans. He used to be a reserve policeman during my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And as reserve police officers, do they only come into duty as an emergency arises or special circumstances?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So they would be on duty at other times as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Do you know Sladan Simic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. The name and surname are familiar. Possibly. He could have also been one of the reserve police officers. I know the name and surname, but I cannot put them to a face.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about Mirko Lakic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Mirko Lakic was never in the reserve police force if we mean the same Mirko Lakic who was constantly at Bikavac as a driver for Centrotrans.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he was never on the reserve police force before you left in April 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how about Mladen Markovic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was his capacity?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: He was on the reserve police force, but I don't know about his job. Maybe he worked in Partizan or some other business.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you weren't always as familiar with all the members of the reserve police force as some, i.e., you knew some more than others?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How about Zivorad Markovic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I know that such a person exists. I know the name and surname, but I can't recall him now. I don't know what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Mile Lakic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to recall. I know the name and surname. Perhaps if you assist me, if you tell me what he was doing, maybe I could tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was he a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There was a Lakic. One Lakic certainly was on the force. I can't remember the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What about Novak Poluga?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I knew him from Preoska Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: As a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: He was not on the force during my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How about Zoran Joksimovic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I know him. He is one of my neighbours. He was on the reserve police force. Sometime before the end of the war. I don't know for how long but I know it was not a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, were you able to actually see, and I would pose this question to the Prosecution to assist me, is the list shown the witness earlier on in -- with Milan Lukic's name on it? Its number is Y019, it's been updated as Y019-1568. And could we have that brought onto the screen, please. Now, sir, you indicated earlier that you had not seen this document before; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: I did see it two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But before two days ago you had not seen it; correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that this is on a regular form of police documentation?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, as for the heading and the format, it looks like an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Including the stamp at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: At that time that stamp was not in use. There was a very big round police stamp. But speaking of stamps, a small police stamp was used in Visegrad by Muslims to designate liquidation. When they put a big stamp it means passage. I have never seen this, though, not before two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in looking at the names on the list, I went through some of the names. Isn't it true that the names that you recognise as reserve police officers, some of them are on this list?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Perica Markovic and all these other names and surnames gravitate towards Visegrad territory, Andric Vidoje, Tasic Zeljko was my colleague, active duty policeman. Lukic Milan was never a policeman. The next one was liquidated a year ago perhaps. He was killed after testifying in Sarajevo. Spasoje Vidakovic, active-duty policeman, he used to be in Sarajevo working as an active-duty policeman, and he had not come to the police station when I was there. I checked his records when he went to the police academy. Novica Savic, the Savic family is dispersed. They live in two or three different places. I can't recognise that. Mladen Andric, I don't know. Nedeljko Gogic, I don't know him personally. Joksimovic, I can't make out the first name, Timotije. I know Joksimovic Timotije was in Kragujevac. I know only one Joksimovic. I'm not sure about the first name. Mirko Lakic, I've explained already. Goran Zecevic was never on the police force during my time. He was working in Switzerland. Sladjan Simic, I know there was one Simic in Koritnik, but whether this is the same person, I'm not sure. Miodrag Bozic, the Bozics live in one part of Visegrad in the Lijesak [phoen] and some others live in the Visegrad-Zupa. Mile Lakic, I've already explained. Anything else you want to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so some of them were reserve police officers before you left, before your time there in Visegrad, correct?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the rest, you would not know if they came on after you left because you were not -- you did not have access to those records after your departure?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No further questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Your Honour, one moment. Could we introduce the last document that we put in, the Y019-1568. We'd like to introduce it as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be admitted as Exhibit 1D25, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kurspahic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My name is Djuro Cepic, and I appear here for Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Nice to meet you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you anything, I want to say on behalf of my entire team that we sympathise with you, and we want to express our condolences for the deaths of your family members in that tragic incident. My client Sredoje Lukic is very sorry, but he's unable to address you directly but those are the rules of the Court. He has no opportunity to ask you any questions himself. He only stood up in order to look you in the eyes. Mr. Kurspahic, I maintain to you that my client Mr. Sredoje Lukic, on the 14th of June, 1992, was not in Pionirska Street. He was not in Visegrad, and he had no part in that incident. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: May I ask you, were you there on that fateful day in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness. Witness, it is not for you to ask questions. Your role is to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You've told us that you had worked with Sredoje Lukic for ten years.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Sredoje Lukic was a good colleague and he socialized equally with Serbs and Muslims alike?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As far as you are concerned, did Sredoje Lukic always express his respect for you and said that you are a good head of your family?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember that his first child was born in a Muslim house while he was living with your common colleague, Taib Barukdzic?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you also recall that he also had Kustur Hajira [phoen] among his friends? He was another one of your colleagues, and they even travelled to the seaside together.

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were all friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the Vasiljevic case you said your father knew Sredoje Lukic very well?

utterances.speaker: HUSO KURSPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
